steps.label: Nitrogen's half-filled stability

A half-filled subshell has extra stability, so
removing an electron from it needs more
steps.why: The general period trend says oxygen, one place to the right, should have the higher ionisation enthalpy — the half-filled 2p³ arrangement of nitrogen is what overrides the trend.
common_mistakes: Arguing from atomic size. Size favours oxygen; the half-filled configuration is what decides this pair.
Writing 2p³ as a pair plus a single electron. It is one electron in each of the three orbitals.
steps.memory_tip: 2p³ is one electron in each of the three orbitals — a half-filled, extra stable arrangement, so removing an electron needs more energy.
steps.margin_note: Write the configurations first; the whole answer reads off them.

steps.label: Oxygen's paired repulsion
lines: In oxygen (2s² 2p⁴) one 2p orbital holds a
The repulsion between the paired electrons
makes one of them easier to remove.

lines.text: IE₁ of N > IE₁ of O

steps.why: The fourth 2p electron of oxygen has no empty orbital left and must pair up; the pair's mutual repulsion raises that electron's energy, so less outside energy is needed to remove it.
common_mistakes: Explaining only nitrogen and never saying why oxygen loses its electron more easily.
Writing the final comparison the wrong way. Nitrogen has the higher first ionisation enthalpy.
steps.memory_tip: Oxygen's fourth p electron must share an orbital; the sharing repulsion makes it the easy one to remove.
steps.margin_note: Both halves are needed: nitrogen's stability and oxygen's repulsion, then the boxed comparison.
